title: Stop Fishing for Compliments
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article dissects the social tactic of fishing for compliments, in which someone disparages themselves purely to bait others into contradicting them with praise. It walks through several concrete, everyday examples of the maneuver in action, from the falsely humble colleague to the appearance-fisher, showing how transparent and manipulative the pattern actually is once named. The piece distinguishes occasional, harmless validation-seeking from a chronic pattern that signals deeper insecurity and even narcissism. It closes by contrasting fishing with genuinely seeking feedback for growth, arguing the latter is what confident leaders actually do.
points: Fishing for compliments works by disparaging a genuine strength in order to bait a contradicting compliment from others.
The tactic is disingenuous by design, and a chronic pattern of it signals underlying insecurity or narcissism, not just a bad habit.
Occasional validation-seeking is normal, but leaders should distinguish it clearly from a repeated pattern that undermines credibility.
Genuinely asking for feedback to improve is different from fishing — the former is a learning tool, the latter is self-affirmation in disguise.
quotes: But those who crave admiration often go too far and seek attention in a way that reveals a deep insecurity.
This manipulative sleight of hand occurs when a person says something negative about themselves in the hope that the other party will disagree and confirm the opposite.
By suggesting they have a weakness that is clearly a strength, they goad others into recognizing their strongest attributes.

But a pattern of deep sea fishing suggests a highly manipulative and narcissistic individual who seeks compliments to bolster an underlying insecurity that portends other cracks in their leadership psyche.
For the best among us, the idea is not about fishing for praise, but in learning how others honestly see us and our performance.
No one worth following should need to have their strengths continually recognized by others.
